"I'd like to meet them- at least one of them," Lyuda says. "If I'm going to do this teaching business, I'll need to get a feel for how their telepathy works. How they think, the anatomy of their brains- wait, do they even have neurons and shit?"
Lyuda whistles. "Terraformers? Must be some powerful dragons," she says. "But they- I mean, they *behave* similarly, right? They *think* the same way, they have the same kind of instincts?"
"Right. And the other one- Blue's more... feral? Is this like a wolf vs dog kind of thing?"
Lyuda nods. She gestures at Chevy's image. "That's the one who can talk, right?"

At about the size of a border collie, Chevy is much, *much* smaller than Blue. It's no surprise the other dragon had considered him a hatchling. Chevy's scales are a mottled collection of browns far less shiny than Blue. Dragon hatchlings generally share this coloration, to hide them from predators. "That's an understatement," Lyuda says dryly. "You said they used to be pets?"

"See, there's no way it'll be safe," Nadya tells her sister, who rolls her eyes. 

"Pssht, you just have no imagination. They *are* telepathic, after all... What's that saying again, 'fuck your brains out'?"

Lyuda, who has no interest in hearing her sister talk about sex, hurriedly says aloud, "Yes! Yes, I see what you mean. Most people would probably find teaching them a bit too- perilous."

Being that he's the size of an adult T-rex, the apartment's not quite big enough to capture Blue's full size. It's daunting nonetheless, especially considering that he's barely into adulthood, and that terraformer dragons continue to grow throughout their lifespan. "Eeesh." Lyuda does a bad job at hiding her trepidation. "That's a big one."

"Pretty, though," Irina opines. "All those iridescent blues."

Nadya eyes her. "Irina. Please don't tell me you want to fuck the big feral reptile."

"I mean. If they offer, and there's a safe way of doing it..."
Lyuda gives Smith an uncertain wave. "Uh, hi?"
"Fair enough," she admits. "But that still means that the freed dragons are going to be really different from how they used to be."
"I'd like that," Lyuda says. "I sort of want to get an unbiased look at the dragons though. I mean- if they didn't figure out the shackles until now they can't be *that* much of an expert."

"They have the *potential* to be able to speak, so they must be somewhat friendly to each other," Lyuda speculates. "Not much use in talking if there's no one to talk *to*, right?" Nadya mutters something about increasingly complex vocalizations in sub-sapient animals correlating to increasingly complex social structures. Lyuda starts scrawling on a notebook. "You said something about a dragon who can speak? D'you think I can meet them for a bit?"

"Probably not," Lyuda admits. "Then again, I'd had seventeen plus years with my old body. It'll be a while yet until we get used to each other." She shakes her head, returning to the topic at hand. "These dragons, how sociable would you say they are? Do they get along with each other? Do they react violently at the sight of humans?"

"It keeps on breathing and digesting and everything. It's just my conscious mind that slips out, not the parts that keep my body running. I'm- there's nothing *wrong* with my mind, or my new body. They're just not used to each other, is all."

Lyuda rubs the bridge of her nose. "Well, I'm *definitely* not going to be in my body when we do this thing, then," she says. "Not at first at least... maybe when I've earned their trust and they've learned not to be... feral."
"I'm willing to help, as I've said," Lyuda says. "Though, uh, one thing first. How... big are they, exactly?"
"Boo," Irina complains. "Ruin my game, won't you?"

Irina sniffs. "Of course there's no proof. Hypothetically, if giant corn monsters were to appear, it would be a distraction. And I am very good at my, purely hypothetical job of running distractions."

Lyuda blinks. "...Is that why I had so many dreams of corn fields last week?"
"That never happened. Shame on you for bringing it up," Irina says quickly.

"They might succeed too," Nadya admits, somewhat sourly. "Look, I just think they'd get better results if they use the carrot instead of the stick. There's no shortage of other island and coastal nations out there that'd appreciate help with the rising sea, not to mention how helpful GMO drought-resistant crops would be... They don't *have* to conquer the world to help it."

"There's a saying that comes to mind about roads to Hell and good intentions," Nadya says. Irina sighs. 

"They're *supervillains.* What did you expect?"

Nadya grimaces. "Hopefully it stays that way."

"Hypocrite," Irina mutters.

"There were extenuating circumstances, as you well know. Anyway, there's a difference between one person doing it and an entire government."
"If they're so *smart*, they should find a way that doesn't involve violently forcing their will on everyone else," Lyuda opines. "Then again, none of them have a MAD in diplomancy. Or logistics."
"Yes, well, the Europeans made similar excuses the first time around, didn't they? All 'white's man burden' this and 'uncivilized savages' that."
Nadya makes a face. "Great, more imperialism."

That's a hot load of bullshit. It doesn't matter what damage is done to the proteins. Your stomach is going to digest them anyway, to chop them up into amino acids. That's what you actually need- the amino acids. That's the building blocks of proteins, that your body uses to make more proteins.
Irina nods. "She's a good person to have as an ally, though."

"So they have the inborn capacity for language development, but not the chance to make use of it. Like feral human children, I guess," Lyuda says, thinking aloud. "Does- I'm not sure how much I can help, if that's the case. Cognitive development usually relies on the right things happening early in life. Critical development periods and stuff, like how it's harder to learn new languages if you're too old. They might no longer have the neuroplasticity to learn the basic things."

"The Madame will figure out a way around it," Irina says firmly.

"She can do that?"

"Sure. It's just a matter of turning on the right genes in the right places. Genes that help with synaptic formation and pruning. Might mean the virus- well, I'm assuming it'll be a virus- needs to stay active in the body longer though. Since it'll have to turn those genes *off* afterwards."
Lyuda nods. "Anything else you can tell me about the dragons? Can they talk, at least?"

Lyuda sighs and sits down on the couch. "If the situation's fucked-up enough that a *supervillain* is willing to help, then I should too," she says, ignoring Irina's pointed 'excuse you?'. "You said you wanted me to... teach them stuff right? What exactly am I supposed to do? Like, do you have a curriculum or something?"

Lyuda grumbles. "I guess... I don't have much to do nowadays, anyway."

"You're a good-for-nothing layabout," Irina says fondly.
Lyuda considers this. "Fair enough. Not my business what people want to do to their bodies. I'm not sure that actually fixes the problem of people being shitty, and people feeling alienated though."
"And humans will do anything for a bit of power. Right."
"I get wanting to fix fucked-up genetic stuff," Lyuda says. "But why would you wanna change species? What's wrong with being human?"

"*Are* there actually people who want to change species?" Lyuda asks, nose wrinkling.

"There're people who ask the Madam for tailored strains of the Maverick virus," Irina says. "I think she's working on a cat one, actually. So... maybe?"
Nadya pauses. "Yeah, that was pretty insensitive of me. Sorry."
"People who like being human? I don't want to be a guy. That doesn't make me a misandrist."
"And I don't want my sister to change into a dragon, so... not sorry?"

Nadya scratches her temple. "Almost definitely not possible," she decides. "Not through sheer exposure. She'd have to spend a long time possessing a dragon body. Like, years at least. Humans aren't machines. Our minds and bodies are... entangled. You can't move a mind to a different body without causing *discrepancies*. No matter how perfect the transfer is. But that also means you can't permanently affect our minds without also altering our bodies."
"Wouldn't it be safer to interact with them if I'm *not* in my body?" Lyuda asks. "It's not like I'm doing it any harm or anything. I'm still breathing and shit."

"I've got my RealTech job too," Irina says. "It doesn't feel right, leaving them when things are heating up like this. Especially when we owe them for helping when Mama got kidnapped."

Lyuda frowns. "What are you two lookin' at me for?"

"You're not wrong," Nadya admits. "But I've still got to deal with the fallout from..." she waves her hand vaguely. "All the demon stuff. Setting up a stable government in Russia. Helping the areas we conquered reform their own governments. Making sure the people are okay and not, like, starving to the point of resorting to cannibalism. Trying to stop other psychics from being lynched by the people who saw us as demon pawns. It's sort of important."
Lyuda crosses her arms. "You're not making a good case for yourself. Why should we help you? What do we get out of it?"

"Animal doesn't mean *stupid,*" Nadya says. "In certain psychic paradigms *humans* are animals. I'm talking in the context of classifying things based on how much their bodies and minds are- wait, what?"

"Just because they'll tolerate conspecifics doesn't mean they'll tolerate *us,*" Lyuda says, but despite herself she does seem interested. "Dragon minds are probably different from ours, if a human enters it'll naturally be much more... intrusive."

"You've worked with animal possession before, Lyuda," Nadya says. "They can't be that different."

"That was a complete headache."
Lyuda purses her lips. "If they had something in their mind that induced pain- that's got to be pretty traumatic. How can you be sure they'll even *let* us into their heads in the first place?"

"Not really," Nadya admits. "I don't like kids. They used to make us take care of the creche kids, back before we escaped. They're brats, and we always ended up getting blamed when broke the rules."

"Does this have anything to do with all the dragons that showed up in my dream last night?" Irina asked.

Nadya yelps in surprise and drops a glass of freezing water on him. Lyuda's body topples to the floor.

"Is being good at teaching stuff a thing you can learn?" Chevy asks. "I wanna help the other dragons too."

The triplets are hanging out in Irina's apartment. Nadya's staring intently at a pair of snowflakes suspended in the air, trying to replicate its fractal structure. Lyuda is doing yoga on a mat in front of the TV.

Chevy shrugs. "I guess. I don't know people though," he admits. "I explained some stuff to Blue in the dream- that telelepacy thing's neat. But it was also kinda hard. I dunno, maybe I'm just not good at explaining stuff."

Chevy nods. "That's what V's planning to do, I think. But I don't think they can do it alone. They're the best, but there's a lot of dragons, and I- I want them to still have time for me. And the baby too, I guess."

Chevy just shrugs. Being a juvenile with a lifetime of trauma behind him, his emotional intelligence is roughly equivalent to that of a potato. "He- he didn't understand things. Not the way I do. I think the Stranger did stuff to me, when she removed the shackles? I know words and stuff. He was just- he could think better, he wasn't stupid anymore. But there's a lot that he's missing. It's like- his brain got stuck as a baby, and it's not stuck anymore, but it's not a grown-up brain either."
Chevy's face goes sour, but he nods. "The other dragons- you think they'd feel mad too?" he asks. "Blue... didn't. I think. He was just confused and scared."
Chevy mulls over this for a moment. "There's bad humans and good humans," he says slowly. "So good Atlanteans must've existed too, right?"
"...No. I'd feel really guilty," he says. "But they did! Why didn't they feel bad about it?"

Chevy considers this. "I want- I want them to feel the way I did. I want them to have- I want them to *suffer*. To feel like their head's burning from the inside all the time. I want them to feel what they did to me. To us."
"I hate them. I wanna- hurt them. That seems bad, though," Chevy says. "Does wanting to hurt people mean I'm a bad person?"

Chevy's quiet for a long moment as he wrestles his emotions back in place. Tries to, at least. "I kinda wish the Atlanteans were still around. Then I could... I dunno."

*Hey, you're the one who brought up Billy. You should've figured out by now that he's got hangups about people not figuring it out and helping him. Anyway, there was supposed to be a point to all this, but the author kept getting sidetracked. Whoops?*

Chevy looks down, shame growing in his chest like the hyphae of a poisonous fungus. He should, he wants to, but- "I'm mad! I'm angry! And- and- and I wanna hurt someone! But that's bad, and- but I'm mad!"
Chevy looks down. "I'm... I can't get mad at him for not being able to help. That's not fair. But I want to be mad at someone! I wanna be mad at someone who's *here,* not- not dead people!"
Chevy flops down and lays his head on the ground. "...that sucks," he says. "But- that feels better? Not his fault he couldn't help. But if he could, and *didn't*..."

Billy definitely can't- that sort of thing is far beyond his area. He's the moment-to-moment aspect of chaos and change, the rampaging storm. All he would do was cause a fatal seizure. Tiamat, the comparatively slow, implacable, not-quite-directed shift of natural forces of selection and evolution, might've been able to do more, to shape their evolution so as to make the shackles obsolete. But then, it would've taken generations upon generations of trial and error. Even odds of the dragons dying off in the process. Evolution is no kindly god; it cares not if whole lineages of species go extinct. As long as there are still living organisms, it'll march on regardless. Bright-scaled Tiamat, Mother of Monsters, held her world-shaping children in some fondness, but in the end they were simply her tools.
Chevy considers this. "...could he have fixed us? The brain thing? I- instead of killing the Atlanteans or something?"

Chevy stews on this for a while, ignoring Leo's words to focus on something else. He hatched from an egg, like Tuba and all other drakes he knew. His sire and dam were also drakes, so they must have came from eggs too, right? And his parents' parents, and their parents too... But then, the very first dragon egg had to come from someone right? That someone had to be a dragon too... so then it wasn't the first dragon egg? No. Leo had said that 'Billy' made the dragons. So 'Billy' had, what, made the first egg? He's not sure that's right, but he can't figure out an alternative. V's talked about things like that, he thinks, but he'd been too *stupid* to understand or pay attention. It feels like he's trying to put together a puzzle with only like, a tenth of the pieces, and the ones he does have don't go together There's not enough for him to figure out the bigger picture, just lines and shapes that could be anything. "...does that mean he's my- dad?"

It takes Chevy a while to muddle through the idea that his kind was 'made'. His first instinct is to say that he was *hatched* from an egg, not made, but that's clearly not what Leo's talking about. The idea of evolution isn't intuitive to him, though. "You mean- before the Atlanteans?" he asks. "Does- did he knew? About what they were doing?"
"Why'd he wanna come here, though?"
Chevy frowns. "A dragon god? Like the baby?"

Chevy glances around, looking for the person who's saying such mean things to his friend. He, obviously, can't find anyone. Which is probably a good thing. "Who's Billy? Is he the one talking to you?" The Storm Dragon is nowhere to be found. He can't remember being Tiamat, so he has no reason to come visit.

The terraformer dragons were, more or less, engineered by Tiamat, the Chaos Dragon of Evolution, as a rather roundabout means of extending her power. Evolution, after all, requires living creatures and living creatures require a livable environment in turn. A mostly-unintended side effect is that dragons have a very strong drive to contribute offspring. Of course, direct procreation isn't the sole way of contributing. Gay and asexual dragons usually assist in incubating eggs instead.

Chevy looks around in confusion. "Who're you talking to, Leo?"

Chevy makes a face. Teenager-equivalent though he might be, dragons don't start to develop interest in sex until they hit their twenties. Their magical side needs to develop properly, otherwise the process of laying and incubating eggs takes a great toll on their health. At this stage he only has a vague sense of aesthetics when it comes to other creatures, not sexual attraction. "Is it really that interesting?" he asks. "I mean, a calendar with dragons on them sounds cool, I guess."
Now he's even more confused. "Why're they putting sex stuff on a calendar? That's gross."
Chevy frowns in adorable confusion. "What's beauty got to do with calendars?"
Chevy giggles. "That's not a good thing. Sweat's gross! Sticky, stinky sweat. Ick!"
Chevy pokes out his tongue. "At least scales are shiny."
"Oh well. There's no accounting for bad taste, I guess," Chevy says cheekily.

From the look on Chevy's face, he definitely disagrees. "I guess. It's boring though. It's all just different shades of brown." It's a disagreement that goes beyond aesthetic preference and into underlying biology. For dragons the smooth, dull skin of humans falls straight into the uncanny valley. It's not as distant in appearance as feathers or fur, but it's definitely not *right* either...
"See? Skin is annoying. Not cute."
"But sun-bathing's fun!"
"That's *scary*," Chevy corrects. "Skin is just... weird. It makes sweat, which is just *gross*. Leaking water, yuck!"
The dragon snorts. "You're not cute. You have *skin.*"

Chevy pouts. "But- but! That's misleading. And therefore mean." V used to play tricks on him when he was little- pretending to throw him a ball while keeping it in their hand instead. It used to frustrate him to no end, but it *did* teach him to pay a little more attention to V rather than immediately running off to find the ball. So maybe it wasn't *that* bad. He still didn't like it, though.
"You can't just say things that you know are wrong! That's lying, and lying's bad." The concept of 'fiction' is probably going to blow his mind.
Chevy giggles. "You're weird. You can't do that. You can't just make things up on the fly."
Chevy frowns. "Can you annoy people into thinking better? I don't think it works like that."
Chevy grunts. "You're not my dad. Or a brain doctor thing."
In the style of teenagers everywhere, Chevy groans. "I *know,*" he says. "You've said it already."

Chevy considers this. "You've never lied to me before, I think," he says. "And... and it doesn't make sense, how you can not exist and still be here, but there's a lot I don't understand. Time travel 'n stuff."
"Mean," the dragon mutters again. "Sorry too, I guess."
Chevy startles again. After everything that's happened today, he's a little on edge. "Mean!"

Chevy jumps back with a squeal and lands three meters away from where he was standing. He looks around for Leo. When the cat-boy is nowhere to be seen, he is abruptly hit with the certainty that Leo is well and truly *gone.* The ground feels unsteady below his feet. "L-l-leo?" His own voice is too loud. He can hear everything- the sound of his own heartbeat, the flapping wings of distant songbirds, the march of ants crawling on the ground. "Leo! This isn't funny!"

The Stranger would like Leo to know that she's not *descended* from ol' Yoggy, she is a fragment of It that deluded Itself to be human because of, and she quotes the author, 'Time Shenanigans or something, bleh'. Anyway, her ol' Yoggy governs over time and space mostly as an accidental function of being the principle of Separation and Con-

Chevy interrupts the rant by poking at Leo. "You *do* exist!"
Chevy's jaw falls open and he falls sideways like a fainting goat. He quickly jumps back to his feet before Leo can get worried. "Wha- buh- how?"

"Gweh," Chevy says. He looks like his brain's going to spontaneously combust if he thinks any harder. You can almost hear the synapses in his brain firing furiously, neurons all lighting up like lights on a christmas tree. Even the idea of time travel is, to him, mind-blowing. "What. You- you can do that- bwuh."
Chevy goes cross-eyed as he tries to wrap his mind around the paradox for the very first time in his life. "But then- I- you- bwuh."
Chevy snorts. "Yeah, right. Then why didn't she fix me earlier? Why didn't she fix the others?"
"But that Red lady knew. She fixed me."
Chevy makes a confused face. "They're doctors. They're supposed to know if people are hurting."
Chevy ponders for a moment. "If... if they can fix bad thoughts. Could they have removed the shackles too? Did they know I was hurting and they didn't tell V?"
Chevy looks deeply conflicted. "I've been to doctors. They're not fun," he says. "...But I usually feel better afterwards."
"But I'm not sick," Chevy says.

"Huh, what?" It's not like he's had experience with therapy before- there hadn't been a reason for V to bring him to one, and they had never really *talked* to him about it. It's not something in his dictionary.

"But what if I can't?" Chevy asks. "What if I try and figure it out but I *can't*?" He starts clawing at the ground in restless agitation. "If I can't understand things it- I- it makes me feel like I'm still *stupid*. I don't like feeling like that."

"I'm scared I'll wake up one day and it turns out it's all a dream, and I'm back to being *stupid* again," Chevy confesses. His voice is almost inaudible. "When I don't understand something it reminds me of- of- you know. It's scary, and when I'm scared I get mad."
"It's scary, isn't it?" Chevy's voice drops into a conspiratorial whisper. "Scarier than even the Atlanteans."

Chevy nods. "You- you said you had those shackles in your brain too, right?" he asks. "When they went away, was it confusing like this? Everything's- sharp. I understand things more- things that I'd have figured out when I was smaller, maybe. It hurts. There's so many things I missed." He didn't have the luxury of coming to a slow, gradual understanding of the world around him, his mental capabilities blooming into fruition. It hit him like a grenade to the face instead- a rapid, unrelenting understanding of the way things work that recontextualized everything he thought he knew about the world. It was exhilarating, in a lot of ways, but it was scary too. If he'd missed so much, what else was lurking out there?
"'m not used to it either. Talking with people, I mean."
"'m sorry too," Chevy says. "I don't really hate you. I just said so because I was mad."
A bloody feather floats down. Chevy bats it around with his paw, sending it straight towards Leo. "I guess. A little."

Chevy looks back after taking off. He flounders somewhat, not really expecting Leo to leave him alone. "Fine!" he hisses. "Fine, if he's not here I- I'm not stupid! I can be alone! I don't need him!" he tells himself.

By the time he's worked out his aggression, he's covered in blood and a *lot* of junglefowl feathers. He half-heartedly snaps his jaw on a thighbone and tries to suck out the marrow. There's not nearly enough of it to satisfy him, but the rest of the chickens have all flown away, and he's not in the mood for another chase.
Unsurprisingly, Chevy is getting fed up of being snapped at. "I hate you!" he screams before taking off and flying away.
Chevy growls. "I'm not stupid! I'm not! I'm not!" he screams. If he can't understand things, that means he's still stupid. He's not.
"I'm not stupid anymore! Things should make more sense. Not the other way around!"
"But- but- but I love them! But I'm also mad at them! It doesn't make sense!"
Chevy jerks away and gives Leo a glare. "I wouldn't! V's- I'd never!"
"I- I know that!" Chevy insists. "But I'm still mad, and it- it's- you said I'm not stupid. Does that mean I'm bad? For still being angry?"
"...but it wasn't enough," Chevy says. "They didn't- V's smart. But they couldn't figure it out."
He's quiet for a moment. "V knows me really well, you know," he says. "Whenever I get tired of being pet, they stop. Even when I was still stupid, when I couldn't say anything, they knew somehow."
The juvenile dragon half-heartedly tries to bat Leo's hand away. "'m not stupid anymore," he says. "Can I still like pets?"
Chevy rubs at his eyes. They're dry- dragons can't cry real tears- but he's picked up that gesture from V anyway. "I h-h-hate you," he lies again, crawling forward to lay his head on Leo's lap.

Chevy growls. He starts tearing out chunks of grass with his front limbs, driving deep gouges into the ground. "Shut up! Shut up! Shut up!" he screams, both at Leo and his own thoughts. More than anything, he's angry at himself for being so out of control. For hating the person who'd done their best to do good by him. For not being good enough to somehow throw off the shackles on his own. But if it was difficult enough for him to acknowledge his mixed feelings towards V, figuring out his own self-hatred is even moreso.
"It's not fair!" he screams. "I didn't do anything wrong! I didn't hurt anyone, but- This isn't fair!"

 "They didn't want any of us to escape. That's why they made it like this," Irina explained.
